title: My Realistic Morning Routine as a Night Owl
creator: Hannah Voss
description:

sentences.t: Good morning, or, well, it's nine forty, which for me is the crack of dawn.
I've tried so many of those five a.m. routines, and every single one of them lasted about three days.
So this is the routine I've actually kept for a year, built for someone whose brain does not work before ten.
Before we start, this video is sponsored by two companies I actually use every morning, so let me tell you about both.

If you go to drinkag1.com/hannah, you'll get a free welcome kit and a year's supply of vitamin D with your first order.
And the second is Paperlane, who send me a new journal and a little stationery bundle every month.
Every box has a notebook with a different paper, a couple of pens, and some stickers that I absolutely do not need but love anyway.
The paper is thick enough that fountain pen ink doesn't bleed through, which, if you journal, you know is rare.
Use code HANNAH20 at paperlane.co for twenty percent off your first box.
Okay, step one of the actual routine, I do not look at my phone until I'm out of bed.
My phone charges across the room, so I physically have to get up to turn off the alarm.
It's rude, but it works.
Step two, I open every curtain in the apartment, because light is the only thing that convinces my body it's daytime.
In winter I'll even sit by the window for ten minutes with my coffee, it makes a huge difference to how awake I feel.
Step three is coffee, obviously, and I make it slowly on purpose.
I grind the beans by hand, I heat the water, I stand there and wait, and it gives my brain about five minutes to catch up with my body.
Step four is my morning pages, which is where I write three pages of whatever is in my head, no editing.
Some days it's a to-do list, some days it's a weird dream I had, some days it's just me complaining about my neighbor's dog.
It sounds pointless, but it clears out all the mental noise before I start working.
Step five, I do a ten-minute stretch, not a workout, just enough to stop feeling like a folded lawn chair.
Cat cow, a couple of hip openers, and lying on the floor staring at the ceiling, which I count as stretching.
And finally, step six, I pick my one thing for the day.
Not a list of twenty tasks, just the one thing that would make today feel like a win if it's the only thing I get done.
I write it on a sticky note and put it on my laptop.
Today it's, finish editing this video, so if you're watching this, it worked.
The whole routine takes about an hour, and it starts whenever I wake up, not at some magic time.
If you're a night owl too, tell me in the comments what helps you get going, because I'm always looking for new ideas.
See you next week!
